subject: biotechnology
title: Fermentation: Yeast Converts Glucose to Ethanol and Carbon Dioxide
objectives: Explain fermentation as the yeast converting glucose into ethanol and carbon dioxide
Run the conversion in order: glucose full, glucose falls, glucose low, glucose used up
Explain why no product appears from nothing: the glucose falls by the amount converted

definitions.meaning: The conversion carried out by yeast in this flask: glucose is taken in and converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide.
The living organism added to the flask: its cells take in glucose and convert it during fermentation.
The sugar in the solution at the start: the glucose bar begins full and falls as the yeast consumes it.
The alcohol produced by fermentation: it appears in the liquid and its bar rises as glucose is converted.
The gas produced by fermentation: bubbles form in the liquid, rise and collect in the gas space.
Material changing into other material, not appearing from nothing: glucose falls by exactly the amount converted into ethanol and carbon dioxide.

mechanismSteps: Add yeast: living cells enter the glucose solution - yeast is added to the glucose solution, the glucose bar is full and there is no ethanol yet (s1).

Fermentation begins: glucose falls, ethanol and gas appear - the yeast takes in glucose, the glucose bar begins to fall, ethanol appears in the liquid and carbon dioxide bubbles rise to the gas space (s2).
Conversion continues: glucose low, ethanol and gas grow - more glucose is converted, the glucose bar is low, the ethanol bar keeps rising and more carbon dioxide collects above the liquid (s3).

Complete: glucose used up, ethanol and carbon dioxide produced - the glucose is almost gone because it was converted, the ethanol bar is high and the gas space is full of collected carbon dioxide (s4).
workedExample: Work through the whole conversion in order. Step 1 (s1): glucose full - yeast is added to the glucose solution and nothing has been converted yet. Step 2 (s2): glucose falls - the yeast takes it in, ethanol appears and carbon dioxide bubbles rise. Step 3 (s3): glucose low - the ethanol bar keeps rising and the gas space fills. Step 4 (s4): glucose used up - the ethanol bar is high and the gas space is full of carbon dioxide. At every stage the order is the same: glucose full, glucose falls, glucose low, glucose used up, and what links them is conversion by the yeast, not products appearing from nothing.

trap.misconception: The alcohol appears from nothing as the mixture ferments, because the glucose in the flask stays the same while ethanol and gas are produced.
trap.explanation: The slip: Ethanol and bubbles appear where none were visible before, so it is easy to think they were created from nothing while the glucose stayed unchanged. The fix: The yeast converts the glucose: as fermentation proceeds the glucose is used up, and that same material reappears as ethanol in the liquid and carbon dioxide gas collecting above it - glucose falls by the amount converted. In class, replay scene 2: freeze as the first bubbles reach the gas space and ask what the glucose bar is doing at that same moment - then run scenes 3 to 4 and watch the glucose fall as the ethanol and gas grow.
